turns.doctor_question: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi Dr. Smith. Well, I guess I came in because... I've been having this strange problem when I try to talk to people. Like, someone will ask me a really simple question at work, like when a ring repair is going to be ready. I'm a jeweler, mostly doing repairs and stone settings these days. I actually started doing that back when I was taking some college classes. The campus had these beautiful flower beds, which is funny because my own garden soil at home is just totally ruined right now. I think it's all the clay, I really need to get some compost down before it gets too cold. 

But anyway... what happens is, I try to answer their question about the ring, and my answer just starts going all over the place. I go from talking about the shop invoices, to the garden soil, and then suddenly I'm rambling about my mortgage papers. And I can just look at the customer's face and see that they're completely losing me. It's embarrassing, really.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient describes their speech going 'all over the place,' jumping from invoices to garden soil to mortgage papers when asked a simple question, which is a clear example of disorganized thinking and speech (derailment/tangentiality).

turns.doctor_question: Aside from this trouble with your train of thought, have you noticed any significant changes in your mood, such as feeling unusually high, energetic, or conversely, extremely low and hopeless?
turns.patient_response: Well, I definitely haven't felt high or energetic... it's really been the opposite. Most mornings, I wake up with this flat, heavy sadness. It's like all the color has drained out of the house before I even get to the shop. Which is a shame, because I used to love the morning light in my kitchen. I have this stained glass piece hanging in the window—a friend made it for me years ago, back when we took a glassblowing workshop together. She was so talented, she actually ended up moving to Seattle to work with glass full-time. I always meant to visit her out there, you know? They say the coffee in Seattle is incredible, though I usually just brew a pot of Folgers at home. It’s cheaper, and honestly, by the time I drink it, it’s cold anyway because I just sit there feeling so weighed down. But yeah, to answer your question, it's just this constant, low feeling.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, wandering from the topic of sadness to stained glass, a friend in Seattle, and coffee before returning to the original point.
symptom_reasoning.S024: The patient reports waking up with a 'flat, heavy sadness' and experiencing a 'constant, low feeling.'
symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient mentions they 'used to love the morning light' but now feel the 'color has drained out,' indicating a loss of pleasure or anhedonia.

turns.doctor_question: Beyond the trouble you have keeping your thoughts on track, have you ever heard, seen, or felt things that others around you do not seem to notice?
turns.patient_response:
Well, I guess... yes, sometimes. Like, when the shop is really quiet, I'll hear this woman muttering my name. It usually sounds like it's coming from the polishing room. We have this big, heavy door on the polishing room because the wheels are so loud, you know? The dust collectors just roar when they're on. I actually had to replace the filters last week, which is such a messy job. The dust gets everywhere, all over your clothes, your hands... I use this special pumice soap to get it off, the kind mechanics use. My dad used to use that soap. He was a mechanic, worked on old Fords mostly. He had this beautiful '65 Mustang he was restoring, cherry red. I always loved that color. It reminds me of rubies, actually. I just set a gorgeous ruby in a vintage platinum band the other day. Platinum is so tricky to work with, you have to get it so incredibly hot. 

But... oh, right, the things I notice. Sometimes I'll also smell burning metal, even when all the torches are completely off. And it feels so real, like the woman's voice, that I actually get up and go check the polishing room or the benches just to be sure nothing is on fire.

symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient describes hearing a woman's voice muttering their name and smelling burning metal when no torches are on, which are clear auditory and olfactory hallucinations.
symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, drifting from the topic of the polishing room to dust filters, pumice soap, their father's car, and setting rubies before finally returning to the doctor's question.

turns.doctor_question: Over the past few months, have you noticed that your mood has been consistently low during the entire time you have been experiencing these issues with your thoughts and hearing that voice, or have there been long stretches where your mood was fine but you were still hearing things or having trouble staying on track?
turns.patient_response:
Well, it hasn't always been both at the same time. I mean, there was a stretch before this heavy sadness really settled in... back when I was still running some jewelry-making classes on the weekends and actually keeping up with my gardening. The garden was doing so well then, I had these amazing heirloom tomatoes. They're so much better than the ones you get at the grocery store, you know? The store ones are just mealy and tasteless because they pick them when they're green and gas them to turn red. It's a real shame. I tried making my own pasta sauce with them once, using this recipe my grandmother gave me. She used to cook everything from scratch, never used a can in her life. She had this huge cast-iron pot that weighed a ton... I actually still have it in my kitchen cupboard, though I don't use it much anymore since I can barely get up the energy to cook. 

But anyway, during that time when I was still doing okay mood-wise, for several weeks I was already hearing those noises from the polishing room. And I was having all this trouble keeping my thoughts straight, worrying that the customers were watching the business and noticing something was wrong with me. So yeah, the voices and the mixed-up talking started before the depression really hit me.

It's one of those memory foam ones, and I think it's starting to lose its shape on my side. I bought it maybe five or six years ago at this big Presidents' Day sale. They always have those sales, don't they? With the guys spinning signs on the street corners. I always wonder how their arms don't get tired doing that all day. It seems like such a strange job to have, just flipping a piece of cardboard around. But I guess a job is a job. I used to think about hiring someone to stand outside the jewelry shop with a sign when we first opened, just to drum up some foot traffic. We're on a side street, so it's easy to miss us if you don't know we're there. We did put out a sandwich board eventually, but the wind kept blowing it over. 

But no, to answer your question... I haven't had any periods where I felt 'up' or energetic like that. Just the low feelings and the voices.

turns.doctor_question: How long has it been since you first started experiencing these voices and the trouble with your thoughts?
turns.patient_response:
Well, let's see... the voices, and smelling the burning metal, and all that worrying about the customers keeping tabs on us... I'd say it started around a year and eight months ago. It was right around the time we were getting ready for the big holiday rush at the shop. The holidays are always so chaotic, you know? Everyone wants custom pieces done at the absolute last minute. I had this one guy come in on Christmas Eve, looking for a custom engraved locket for his wife. Christmas Eve! Can you imagine? I told him there was no way I could get it done, engraving takes time, especially if you want it done right by hand. Hand engraving is a dying art, really. Most places just use lasers now. Lasers are fast, sure, but they don't have the same depth or character as a hand-carved piece. My mentor, who taught me everything I know about setting stones, he was a master engraver. He had these tiny, delicate tools... gravers, they're called. He kept them so sharp you could cut yourself just looking at them. He used to sharpen them on this Arkansas stone with a little drop of oil. The oil smelled a bit like... well, not like the burning metal I smell now, but it had a distinct scent. 

But anyway, yeah, it's been about a year and eight months since all this started.

symptom_reasoning.S020: The patient explicitly mentions experiencing "voices" and "smelling the burning metal," confirming auditory and olfactory hallucinations.

turns.doctor_question: Looking back at the past year and eight months, would you say that the periods where you felt that heavy, low mood have added up to most of that time, or were they just brief episodes that happened every once in a while?
turns.patient_response:
Well, it's definitely been most of the time. It's not just a bad week here or there. For the majority of that year and eight months, this heavy, bleak mood has just been sitting on me... along with the terrible sleep and not wanting to eat, and just this awful guilt about everything. It's just my daily life now. Which is strange, because I used to have such a good appetite, especially for breakfast. I used to make these elaborate breakfasts on Sundays... waffles from scratch, with the egg whites whipped up so they get really fluffy. You have to fold them in so carefully, otherwise you knock all the air out. My mother taught me that. She had this old rotary egg beater, the kind with the crank on the side? I loved turning that handle when I was a little girl. It made this rhythmic clattering sound against the glass bowl. Glass bowls are so much better for whipping egg whites than plastic ones, the plastic always holds onto a little bit of grease and then the eggs won't peak right. I tried to find one of those old rotary beaters at an antique store a few years ago, but they were all rusted or the gears were stripped. It's hard to find good quality kitchen tools anymore, everything is just cheap plastic that breaks after a year. 

But, um, yes... to answer your question, the low mood and everything else, it's been present for almost the whole time.

I had a student do that once with a beautiful piece of sterling silver, just melted right into a blob. Silver is so conductive, it pulls the heat away from the joint so fast, you really have to use a bigger torch tip than you think you need. I always tell them to heat the whole piece first, not just the joint. But they get nervous and focus the flame in one spot. 

But yes, during that time, for those several weeks, I was still teaching and doing my gardening, feeling okay mood-wise, but I was definitely hearing those noises from the polishing room and worrying about the customers watching us.
